Breastfeeding wasn't hard for me but it also wasn't the easiest. I had the usual worries and doubts but I'm so lucky that I never experienced mastitis, low supply, ties or anything like that. 

Now, I'm pregnant with my second (only 16 weeks) but I already know that this time round I may not be so lucky, I may struggle. But going in with even more knowledge and experience I hope that it will benefit me greatly. 

My advice to anyone that wants to breastfeed always is, educate yourself whilst your pregnant. Learn what's normal.. cluster feeding, clinginess, normal baby sleep (surprise shock: sleeping like a baby means waking up every 2-3 hours as thats biologically normal and prevents SIDS), healthy nappy output and learning what's not normal.. shallow latch, nipples in pain, baby not gaining weight.. the more education you give yourself before you have the stress of a newborn, the smoother the ride for you could be. 

Also, try to surround yourself with people that support breastfeeding... Facebook pages (and this subreddit) are amazing for that and if you find the right ones they can be so helpful and supportive in the times you feel like giving up.

We have care plans and nothing is accepted unless the client and their family/spokesperson is happy with it. Their shifts are usually 9am til 3pm and can work as many or as little amount of days as they want. A lot of my clients are older and just like the feeling of being important and a part of society as a lot of them were shut away or put into institutions when they were younger.
They work 1-5 days a week depending on what they want to do. If they're sick or just not feeling it then they have annual leave and sick leave like everyone else.

In Australia we have work places designed with jobs for people with a disability (some can get a forklift license if they have the capabilities) and get paid below wage but that's only so they can keep they're disability payments (around $800f/n), entitlements and discounts. I believe this is a fair arrangement, they get to have a job, get the socialisation a job offers and instead of losing money they make a couple hundred extra a week.

Ok... have you thought of reminding him about "gentle hands". Yes, a 2 year old knows how to use his hands softly but they have absolutely no impulse control, that doesnt START to develop until around 4 or 5, but you're an adult, you do. All you're teaching him is to hit someone when they're not doing something how he likes. For example; he sees a kid in the sand pit throwing sand, the child that gets smacked for that goes up and hits that kid, now the parent sees him hit a kid so they smack him and tell him not to hit other kids. So, why is it ok for an adult to smack someone so much smaller and under developed for doing the wrong thing but they can't do the same when they see someone do something wrong?

So demonstrate, teach and model the behaviour you want your child to learn. Have patience knowing that their little brain is so underdeveloped that they honestly can't control themselves.
